Who Changed the Creator’s Day?

Read, reflect, and take the time you need.

Section 1 of 10

Can human authority change something the Creator made holy?

Governments and religious institutions can make rules. Customs can become so old that people stop asking where they began. But can popularity, tradition, or political power change a command from the Creator?

Native peoples know that an official policy can be powerful and still be wrong. This lesson is not comparing Sabbath history with the terrible harm done to Native communities. It simply recognizes an important truth: human authority does not turn error into truth.

The safest path is to read the Bible and let it speak for itself.

What day did the Creator make holy?

Read Genesis 2:1–3 ↗ and Exodus 20:8–11 ↗.

The Creator rested on the seventh day. He blessed the seventh day and made it holy. In the Ten Commandments, He identifies it as the Sabbath.

The seventh day is Saturday. It begins at sunset Friday and ends at sunset Saturday.

The command does not say, “Choose any day you prefer.” It does not say, “Keep one day out of seven.” It identifies the seventh day.

Jesus kept the Sabbath. Read Luke 4:16 ↗.

After Jesus returned to heaven, His followers continued meeting and teaching on the Sabbath. Read Acts 13:42–44 ↗; Acts 16:13 ↗; Acts 17:2 ↗; and Acts 18:4 ↗.

Jesus also said:

“The Sabbath was made for man.”

Mark 2:27 ↗

The Sabbath was made for humanity—not for only one nation.

Did Jesus change the Sabbath?

Jesus rose from the dead on the first day of the week. His resurrection is the foundation of our hope. But no Gospel says that the first day became holy because Jesus rose on it.

Read Matthew 28:1–6 ↗ and John 20:1, 19 ↗.

The disciples were gathered behind locked doors because they were afraid. The passage does not say they were keeping a new Sabbath.

Jesus said He did not come to destroy the law. Read Matthew 5:17–19 ↗. He warned against setting aside God’s commandments in favor of human tradition. Read Mark 7:7–9 ↗.

If Jesus had changed one of the Ten Commandments, we should expect Him to say so clearly. No such command appears in the Bible.

What about the first-day passages?

Several passages are sometimes used to support Sunday holiness. Look closely at what they actually say.

Acts 20:7 ↗

Believers gathered on the first day, and Paul spoke until midnight. This was a farewell meeting before Paul continued his journey. According to the Bible’s sunset-to-sunset way of counting days, the meeting may have begun on what we call Saturday night.

People also broke bread on other days. Read Acts 2:46 ↗. A meeting on a particular day does not make that day the Sabbath.

1 Corinthians 16:1–2 ↗

Paul asked each believer to set aside money on the first day so it would be ready for a future collection. The passage never calls the first day holy, a Sabbath, or a day of worship.

Colossians 2:14–17 ↗

Paul discusses food, drink, festivals, new moons, and ceremonial sabbath days that pointed forward to Jesus. Those ceremonies were shadows of what Jesus would accomplish.

The seventh-day Sabbath was established at creation, before sin and before the ceremonial system. It points backward to the Creator’s completed work. It also appears in the Ten Commandments, written by God’s own hand.

Romans 14:5–6 ↗

This chapter addresses disagreements about eating, fasting, and personal observances. It does not mention the seventh-day Sabbath or cancel any of the Ten Commandments.

Revelation 1:10 ↗

John says he was “in the Spirit on the Lord’s day,” but he does not name Sunday. Elsewhere, the Creator calls the Sabbath “My holy day,” and Jesus calls Himself “Lord also of the Sabbath.” Read Isaiah 58:13 ↗ and Mark 2:28 ↗.

None of these passages contains a command transferring Sabbath holiness from the seventh day to the first.

How did Sunday become widely observed?

The change did not happen through one clear announcement. It developed gradually.

Some believers began honoring Sunday as a celebration of Jesus’ resurrection. A second-century writer named Justin Martyr described Sunday gatherings. His account shows that the practice had begun in some places, but his writing is not Scripture and does not contain a command from Jesus. You can read the account in Justin Martyr’s First Apology, chapter 67 ↗.

In A.D. 321, Roman Emperor Constantine issued a civil law requiring courts and many city businesses to rest on “the venerable day of the sun.” Farmers were exempt. This law did not come from the Bible, and it was not the Sabbath commandment. It gave Sunday powerful government support. The law is recorded in this history of Constantine’s Sunday decree ↗.

Later in the fourth century, the Council of Laodicea told believers not to rest on the Sabbath but to work that day and honor Sunday instead. Canon 29 preserves that ruling ↗.

Over time, religious tradition and government authority worked together. Sunday observance became normal, while Sabbath observance was discouraged and sometimes punished.

The modern Roman Catholic catechism still says that the Sabbath “has been replaced by Sunday.” That is an honest statement of its tradition, but the catechism’s claim ↗ is based on church authority rather than a Bible command transferring the day.

The historical answer is therefore clear: no apostle changed the Sabbath. Sunday observance grew through custom, religious rulings, and civil power.

Daniel warned that a power would attempt a change

Read Daniel 7:23–25 ↗.

Daniel saw a power that would rise from the Roman world. It would combine political influence with religious claims, oppose the Most High, persecute God’s people, and “intend to change times and law.”

Following Daniel’s sequence, these identifying marks point to the church-state system that developed around papal Rome during the Middle Ages.

This prophecy is not permission to hate Catholics or judge individual people. Many Catholics sincerely love Jesus and live according to the truth they understand. The prophecy examines a system’s claims and actions—not the value of the people within it.

Notice that Daniel says this power would intend, or think, to change God’s law. Human beings can change calendars, traditions, and civil laws. They cannot change what the Creator has made holy.

This is really a question of authority

The deepest question is not simply, “Which day feels right?”

It is:

“Whose word will guide my life?”

Jesus asked a similar question:

“Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do the things which I say?”

Luke 6:46 ↗

The Bible stands above every culture, government, church, and religious leader. It also examines every one of us. No human culture is the standard of truth—not European culture, Native culture, modern popular culture, or religious culture.

The Creator alone has final authority.

What about sincere Sunday worshipers?

Keeping Sunday does not automatically mean someone has rejected God or received the mark of the beast. Many people have never been shown what the Bible teaches about the Sabbath. The Creator knows every heart and understands what each person has had an opportunity to learn.

Revelation describes a future time when worship, authority, and obedience will become a clear worldwide issue. People will be pressured to follow human commands instead of the Creator’s law. The final mark will involve an informed choice under that pressure.

Truth should never be used as a weapon against sincere people. It should lead us to humility, love, and faithfulness.

The Sabbath does not erase who you are

Choosing to keep the Creator’s Sabbath does not require you to become culturally white or reject your nation, family, language, or ancestry.

You do not need to copy another culture’s worship style. You can pray in your own language, sing in ways that are meaningful to your family, share food, spend time with loved ones, help someone in need, and enjoy the Creator’s world.

Different Native nations and families have different histories and customs. The Sabbath does not erase those differences. It gives people from every nation a shared reminder that they were created by the same God and redeemed by the same Jesus.

Following the Creator may require every person to release practices that conflict with His Word. That is true in every culture. But obedience to Jesus is not the destruction of your identity. He calls you to belong fully to Him while honoring the people and history He gave you.

You are free to examine the evidence

You do not have to accept this lesson because someone sounds confident. Read the passages. Ask questions. Compare every claim with the Bible.

The Creator does not need manipulation to defend His truth.

If the seventh day is His Sabbath, the honest response is not, “What does everyone else do?” It is, “Creator, how do You want me to live?”

Think About It

  1. Can a human institution make holy a day that the Creator did not make holy?
  2. Did you find any Bible verse commanding people to keep Sunday as the Sabbath?
  3. Why do you think traditions can become more familiar than the Bible itself?
  4. How can you honor relatives who worship on Sunday while following what you now understand?
  5. What concerns would you need to bring to the Creator before beginning to keep the Sabbath?

Try This During the Coming Week

Day 1

Read Genesis 2:1–3 ↗ and Exodus 20:8–11 ↗.

Write down everything the Creator did to the seventh day.

Day 2

Read Luke 4:16 ↗ and Mark 2:27–28 ↗.

What do Jesus’ words reveal about the purpose of the Sabbath?

Day 3

Read Matthew 28:1–6 ↗ and John 20:19 ↗.

Do these passages contain a command changing the Sabbath?

Day 4

Read Acts 20:7–12 ↗ and 1 Corinthians 16:1–2 ↗.

List what the passages say—and what they do not say.

Day 5

Read Colossians 2:14–17 ↗ and Hebrews 4:4, 9–11 ↗.

Ask the Creator to help you understand the difference between ceremonial shadows and His creation rest.

Day 6

Read Daniel 7:23–25 ↗ and Revelation 14:6–12 ↗.

Notice how creation, worship, commandments, and faithful endurance are connected.

Day 7

Read Psalm 119:97–105 ↗ and Acts 5:29 ↗.

Ask yourself: “Am I willing to follow the Creator’s Word even when tradition says something different?”

A Prayer You Can Pray

Creator, thank You for giving me Your Word. I do not want tradition, fear, or pressure to decide what I believe. Please show me what is true.

Give me courage to follow You without becoming proud or unkind toward people who understand things differently. Help me honor my family and my people while placing Your Word above every human authority.

Jesus, teach me how to receive Your Sabbath as a gift. If changes are needed in my life, guide me one step at a time. I choose to trust You. Amen.

Remember This

No emperor, religious council, or church institution can change what the Creator blessed and made holy.

Sunday observance became widespread through human custom and authority—not through a command from Jesus.

The seventh-day Sabbath remains the Creator’s day. His invitation is not about earning salvation. It is about trusting Him enough to follow His Word.

What does Sabbath keeping look like in real life? The next lesson explores how to prepare for the Sabbath and enjoy it as a day of worship, freedom, family, healing, mercy, and time with the Creator.
